# Results — Study 941 (Short Both Legs) on the real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The trade: per $1 of equity,
sell short **$0.50 of TQQQ** (3x long Nasdaq-100) and **$0.50 of SQQQ** (−3x inverse
Nasdaq-100), reset to equal dollars on a schedule, hold the proceeds and the equity in
cash. Daily total-return closes (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=True`); the cash leg is **BIL**'s
actual total return, and every number below is **excess-of-cash**. One execution lag: the
reset is decided at the close of day t (from the calendar alone) and drives the return of
day t+1. One-way cost 2 bps of traded notional. Common TQQQ∩SQQQ∩QQQ∩BIL window
2010-02-11 → 2026-06-30. As-of **2026-06-30** (the partial current month is dropped).*

> **Read the headline with its cost attached.** Every "harvest" number in this file is
> **before any stock-borrow fee**, because no free borrow-fee history exists. The borrow
> rate is an explicit **ASSUMPTION**, it is swept end to end below, and the *breakeven*
> borrow — not the gross harvest — is the number the verdict rests on.

## Data stamp

| Legs | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| TQQQ, SQQQ (shorted), QQQ (benchmark), BIL (cash) | 2010-02-11 → 2026-06-30 | 4,120 | Fingerprint `8f75619ff8e2` |

**Labelled proxies.** *Cash* is BIL's own total return, i.e. T-bills **net of BIL's expense
ratio**, and the short rebate is modelled as paying exactly that. A real prime-broker
rebate is set off a different benchmark; using BIL understates the harvest by BIL's fee and
by the bill-vs-overnight basis, so this choice errs against the trade rather than for it.

**Survivorship and pair selection — and it does *not* all point one way.** The universe here
is **n = 1**, and it was chosen with full hindsight: TQQQ/SQQQ is the pair everyone means
when they tell this story, and the only 3x long/inverse pair with an unbroken sixteen-year
history on a liquid index. Both funds survived the whole window. The two consequences pull
in **opposite** directions and both are load-bearing:

- *On the signal, it is conservative.* This is the largest, cheapest, best-run levered pair
  in existence. A smaller or sloppier pair — or one of the many levered products that were
  wound up over this period — would almost certainly show a **larger** residual load, so the
  +2.06%/yr measured here is close to a floor across the levered-ETF universe.
- *On the tradability, it is anti-conservative, and this is the one that matters.* This pair
  is also the **easiest and cheapest to borrow** of any levered pair. The borrow assumption
  is therefore being tested on its most favourable possible specimen; any generalisation to
  smaller levered pairs makes the borrow problem **worse**, not better, while the harvest
  grows more slowly than the fee would.

One correction to a claim it is tempting to make (and that an earlier draft of this study
did make): a levered fund being **wound up mid-sample is not a windfall for a short**. An
ETF liquidation pays NAV; the short is simply bought in at NAV and closes flat. What a
closure actually costs a short is the *forced re-entry* — the position ends on the fund's
schedule, not the arbitrageur's. Fund mortality is a nuisance here, not a hidden profit.

## The two legs, and what is actually collectable

Annualised **arithmetic** means over the window (total return, not price-only):

| Leg | Mean | Vol |
|---|--:|--:|
| TQQQ (3x long) | +55.48% | 61.2% |
| SQQQ (−3x inverse) | −57.25% | 61.3% |
| QQQ (index) | +20.30% | 20.7% |
| BIL (cash) | +1.32% | 0.3% |

The two levered legs' *arithmetic* means are ±3x the index plus each fund's own financing
carry and cost load. Shorting half a dollar of each therefore leaves, per year:

> `cash − 0.5 × (TQQQ + SQQQ)` = **+2.20%/yr** — the two funds' average shortfall against a
> costless ±3x replication financed at BIL. The famous volatility decay
> (≈ 3σ² ≈ 13%/yr for the 3x, ≈ 6σ² ≈ 26%/yr for the −3x on QQQ's 21% vol) is a
> **geometric** artefact of the compounded path; a constant-dollar short never touches it.

**Two warnings on that number, both of which the first draft of this study got wrong.**

1. **It is an identity, not a corroboration.** On the daily reset with a full rebate, zero
   borrow and zero cost the simulated book's excess return *is* `cash − 0.5 × (long + short)`,
   day by day, to 5e-16. So "the harvest matches the implied load" is algebra restating
   itself; it is **not** two independent measurements agreeing. What the simulator adds
   beyond the identity is everything that is not algebra — the non-daily schedules, the
   borrow and rebate terms, the trading cost, the compounding of the equity path, and the
   ruin check.
2. **It is a residual, and its name is an interpretation.** The +2.20%/yr is whatever the
   two funds failed to deliver against an idealised ±3x financed at BIL. That bucket
   contains the expense ratios, the financing spread over the funds' true funding rate, the
   funds' own end-of-day rebalancing costs, tracking error, and the BIL-versus-funding
   basis. **This study measures none of those components separately.** Calling the residual
   a "fee load" is consistent with the fund mechanics and with the way it widens in stressed
   years, but it is a reading of a residual, not a fee audit.

### Which leg is the harvest actually coming from?

The same residual, split. A costless `+3x` fund would return `3·r_index − 2·r_cash` on an
average day and a costless `−3x` fund `−3·r_index + 4·r_cash`; what each real fund fails to
deliver against that is its own shortfall, and the pair short collects the **average**:

| Leg | Shortfall vs its costless replication | Share of the harvest |
|---|--:|--:|
| TQQQ (3x long) | **+2.79%/yr** | 63% |
| SQQQ (−3x inverse) | **+1.61%/yr** | 37% |
| Average = the pair harvest | **+2.20%/yr** | 100% |

This is a decomposition of the identity, not a second measurement, and it inherits every
caveat above. But it changes how the borrow number should be read, and not in the trade's
favour. Each leg pays borrow on **its own half** of the notional, so each leg has its own
breakeven equal to its own shortfall — and the thin one is the wrong one. **SQQQ, the
crowded, expensive-to-borrow inverse fund, breaks even at 1.61%/yr**; the 2.06% blended
breakeven only exists because the cheap, general-collateral TQQQ leg (2.79%/yr) subsidises
it. A blended fee of 2%/yr made of 0.5% on TQQQ and 3.5% on SQQQ kills the trade at exactly
the same blended rate as a symmetric 2%/2% — but it is the far more likely shape of the bill,
and it means the leg that is easy to borrow is the only one reliably paying for itself.

What *is* established rather than interpreted: the residual is not the compounding decay.
That is settled by the algebra (`E[r_L] = L·E[r_index] − (L−1)·r_cash − load` carries no σ²
term; the decay lives only in `E[log r_L]`) and demonstrated by the synthetic control below,
where an identical, enormous decay pays exactly nothing once the fee load is set to zero.

## Headline — daily reset, **zero borrow**, 2 bps

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| Excess-of-cash mean (before borrow) | **+2.06%/yr** |
| Excess-of-cash Sharpe | **+1.64** |
| HAC (Newey-West) *t* | **+8.82** |
| Annualised vol | 1.26% |
| Max drawdown | −1.37% |
| Worst day / worst month | −1.14% / −0.23% |
| Skew / excess kurtosis | +1.64 / +47.3 |
| Turnover | 6.8x NAV/yr |
| Residual beta to QQQ | **+0.0032** (R² 0.003) |
| Alpha to QQQ | +2.00%/yr (*t* = +8.49) |

Bootstrap (2,000 draws, 21-day blocks): Sharpe **+1.64**, 95% CI **[+1.36, +1.90]**;
mean **+2.06%/yr**, 95% CI **[+1.67%, +2.64%]**, 0.0% of resamples below zero. QQQ's own
excess-of-cash Sharpe over the same window is +0.92 — the pair short is genuinely neutral
to it, not a disguised long: of the +2.06%, only +0.06 pp is the residual beta, leaving
+2.00%/yr of market-neutral alpha.

A *t* of +8.82 on a series this thin (1.26% vol) is not the discovery of an anomaly; it is
a statement that a **cost accrual is stable**. That is exactly what one should expect if
the residual is what we think it is, and it is why the size of the number — not its
significance — is the thing that matters here.

## Is it an accrual, or a handful of days?

The excess series has +47 excess kurtosis, so this is the test that decides whether the
"steady fee accrual" story survives:

| Cut | Mean | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| Full sample | +2.06%/yr | +8.82 |
| Median day (annualised) | +1.74%/yr | — |
| 1% two-sided trimmed mean | +1.82%/yr | — |
| Drop the 5 best days (14.2% of the total) | +1.77%/yr | +13.48 |
| Drop the 20 best days (32.5%) | +1.40%/yr | +9.60 |
| Drop the 50 best days (54.2%) | +0.95%/yr | +5.53 |
| Excluding 2020 entirely | +1.77%/yr | +15.97 |

**Read the mean column, not the *t* column.** Deleting the best observations and then
re-running a *t*-test is not valid inference: it strips the right tail, so the *t* rises
**mechanically** (+8.82 → +13.48 after removing five days) even while the mean falls. Those
*t*'s measure how smooth what is left is; they are not significance tests, and nothing in
the verdict rests on them. The same applies to the 2020 exclusion, where dropping the most
volatile year of the sample is what takes the *t* to +15.97.

55.9% of days are positive and the median day annualises to +1.74%. The fat right tail is
real — the biggest days are 2010-08-10 and the March 2020 crash week, exactly when the
funds' own end-of-day rebalancing is most expensive — but the trade is **not** a tail bet:
throwing away the fifty best days out of 4,119 still leaves +0.95%/yr at *t* = +5.5. It
also, note, leaves the trade **below its own breakeven borrow**.

## Rebalance schedule — the short-gamma dial

| Reset | Mean | Sharpe | Vol | HAC *t* | Max DD | Worst month | Beta | Max gross | Ruined |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| daily | +2.06% | **+1.64** | 1.3% | +8.82 | −1.4% | −0.2% | +0.003 | 1.0x | no |
| weekly | +2.69% | +0.55 | 4.9% | +2.18 | −11.4% | −7.1% | +0.030 | 1.1x | no |
| monthly | +5.26% | +0.44 | 11.8% | +2.39 | −15.5% | −12.1% | +0.190 | 1.3x | no |
| never | −61.15% | −0.49 | 124.8% | −0.81 | **−100.0%** | −100.0% | −3.345 | 51.7x | **yes (2013-08-01)** |

Letting the book drift looks like it pays more, but the extra return is **not** extra
harvest: monthly's alpha to QQQ is +1.64%/yr with *t* = **+0.68** — its headline +5.26%
is mostly the +0.19 residual beta collecting the Nasdaq's own excess return. The Sharpe
*falls* by a factor of four and the worst month goes from −0.2% to −12.1%. Never
rebalancing is not a strategy at all: the 3x leg compounds away from the short faster than
the inverse leg dies, the gross short reaches **51.7x NAV**, and the book is wiped out on
**2013-08-01**.

## The crux — borrow (an ASSUMPTION, swept, never asserted)

There is no free history of stock-borrow fees, so the borrow rate is a **PROXY /
ASSUMPTION** applied to the gross short notional (1.0x NAV) and swept end to end:

| Assumed blended borrow | Mean | Sharpe | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0%/yr (the headline above) | +2.06% | +1.64 | +8.82 |
| 1%/yr | +1.06% | +0.84 | +4.54 |
| **2%/yr** | **+0.06%** | +0.05 | +0.26 |
| 3%/yr | −0.94% | −0.75 | −4.02 |
| 5%/yr | −2.94% | −2.34 | −12.57 |
| 8%/yr | −5.94% | −4.72 | −25.40 |
| 15%/yr | −12.94% | −10.28 | −55.35 |

**Breakeven blended borrow: 2.06%/yr** on the daily reset (2.70% weekly, 5.27% monthly —
but the weekly and monthly versions buy that headroom with the tail above). TQQQ is a
$20bn+ general-collateral name that borrows cheaply; SQQQ is the crowded side, and the
blended fee across the pair sits *around* the breakeven rather than safely below it. That
the fee and the edge are the same size is not a coincidence — it is what the securities-
lending literature predicts when the reason to short a security is mechanical and public.

## Account terms — the short rebate is a precondition, not a source

| Terms | Mean | Sharpe | HAC *t* | Breakeven borrow | 2010–2017 | 2018–2026 |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Full rebate (prime broker) | +2.06% | +1.64 | +8.82 | 2.06%/yr | +1.50% (*t* +7.98) | +2.59% (*t* +6.39) |
| **No rebate (retail)** | +0.75% | +0.60 | +3.02 | **0.75%/yr** | +1.45% (*t* +7.86) | **+0.10% (*t* +0.22)** |

The rebate is **not a component of the alpha**: the two legs' own financing carry averages
to +1x cash on the liability side, and the interest on the short proceeds is what offsets
it. With a full rebate the excess return is the residual load, in full. What a retail
account without a rebate does is *forfeit the cash rate itself* — **1.32%/yr on this
sample** — which is a cost of the account terms. It happens to be worth more than half the
harvest, and it grows with the level of rates: since 2018 it takes the trade to
**+0.10%/yr, *t* = +0.22**, i.e. nothing at all.

| Cost | Mean | Sharpe | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +2.20% | +1.74 | +9.31 |
| 2 bps (headline) | +2.06% | +1.64 | +8.82 |
| 5 bps | +1.86% | +1.48 | +8.06 |
| 10 bps | +1.52% | +1.21 | +6.74 |

Turnover is 6.8x NAV/yr, so trading friction costs ~7 bps per bp of one-way cost. Cost is
not what kills this trade; borrow is.

## Calendar-year excess-of-cash (daily reset, 2 bps, zero borrow)

| Year | Excess | Worst day | | Year | Excess | Worst day |
|---|--:|--:|---|---|--:|--:|
| 2010 | +2.23% | −1.14% | | 2019 | +1.58% | −0.22% |
| 2011 | +2.35% | −0.27% | | 2020 | **+6.79%** | −0.57% |
| 2012 | +1.53% | −0.32% | | 2021 | +1.65% | −0.19% |
| 2013 | +1.22% | −0.30% | | 2022 | +3.63% | −0.26% |
| 2014 | +1.32% | −0.20% | | 2023 | +2.49% | −0.14% |
| 2015 | +1.14% | −0.58% | | 2024 | +2.00% | −0.19% |
| 2016 | +0.92% | −0.25% | | 2025 | +2.31% | −0.07% |
| 2017 | +1.09% | −0.17% | | 2026 (H1, partial) | +0.76% | −0.18% |

Every single year is positive before borrow — but the size moves with market stress
(2020: +6.79%, 2022: +3.63%), which is what one expects if the residual is the funds' own
costs, since those widen when the index whips. Note also that **eleven of the seventeen
years sit below the 2.06% breakeven borrow** (only 2010, 2011, 2020, 2022, 2023 and 2025
clear it): "positive every year" and "profitable every year" are not the same claim, and
the median year is the one that loses money once the borrow is paid.

## Synthetic control (machinery proof only — never supports the stamp)

Both synthetic worlds carry the **same** enormous decay in their levered legs (14.5%/yr in
the 3x, 29.0%/yr in the −3x); the only difference is whether the funds charge a fee.

| World | Planted harvest | Recovered | max \|*t*\| over 6 seeds |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Costly funds | +2.45%/yr | **+2.45%/yr** (sd 0.00%) | 15.06 |
| Free funds (null) | 0.00%/yr | **+0.00%/yr** | 0.05 |

The detector recovers a planted fee load and stays silent when the fee is removed **even
though the decay is untouched** — the study's central point stated as a controlled
experiment: the decay is not collectable by a constant-dollar short; a cost load is. These
are synthetic numbers and they support the *machinery*, never the stamp.

## Verdict

- **Signal — Real.** Before borrow, the daily-reset pair short delivers a market-neutral
  excess-of-cash return of **+2.06%/yr** (alpha to QQQ +2.00%/yr) with HAC *t* = **+8.82**,
  a bootstrap mean CI of [+1.67%, +2.64%] clear of zero, residual beta **+0.003**, positive
  in every calendar year, in both eras (+1.50% *t* +7.98 / +2.59% *t* +6.39), and surviving
  the removal of its fifty best days (+0.95%/yr) and of 2020 entirely (+1.77%/yr) — those
  two cuts are magnitude checks, not significance tests. The effect is real and stable. It
  is **not the decay**: it is the two funds' residual shortfall against a costless ±3x
  replication — a cost load, on the most natural reading of a residual this study does not
  decompose. The BIL cash proxy points the conservative way, and so does pair selection
  *for the signal*: this is the cheapest, best-run levered pair, so its residual is close to
  a floor.
- **Tradability — Fragile.** The entire edge lives inside the borrow assumption: breakeven
  blended borrow is **2.06%/yr** against a pair that is half crowded-short SQQQ — whose own
  leg breaks even at just **1.61%/yr**, the cheap TQQQ leg carrying 63% of the harvest — and
  no free borrow-fee tape exists to settle it. Pair selection runs **against** the trade
  here: TQQQ/SQQQ is the easiest and cheapest levered pair in the world to borrow, so this
  is the borrow assumption's most favourable possible specimen and nothing here generalises
  to a smaller pair. At retail terms (no interest on the short proceeds)
  the trade earns **+0.75%/yr** overall and **+0.10%/yr, *t* = +0.22, since 2018** — for a
  retail account this is a Mirage, not a Fragile. Nor can the return be scaled up by
  rebalancing less: monthly triples the headline but its alpha *t* falls to +0.68, its
  Sharpe to +0.44 and its worst month to −12.1%, and an unrebalanced book is destroyed
  outright (2013-08-01, gross short 51.7x). What is left, in the best case, is a 1.3%-vol
  prime-brokerage carry worth ~2%/yr before a borrow fee that exists precisely to price it
  away.
